keyVerseText: For whatsoever things were written aforetime were written for our learning, that we through patience and comfort of the scriptures might have hope.
rootMeaning: The Greek verb προγράφω (prográphō) is formed from the prefix πρό (pró), meaning "before" or "prior to," and the root γράφω (graphō), meaning "to write." Literally, it conveys the idea of "writing beforehand" or "writing in advance." This etymology highlights a temporal and authoritative aspect—something is not merely written, but recorded prior to an event or made publicly known ahead of time. This adds depth beyond the English glosses by emphasizing foreordination or prior declaration.
usageInScripture: In Scripture, προγράφω appears in contexts where something has been "written before," "ordained," or "set forth evidently." It occurs five times with translations including "were written," "hath been evidently set forth," "I wrote afore," and "ordained." This consistency shows the word's core use in referring to authoritative writings or decrees established in advance, often carrying the implication of divine purpose or public proclamation. The range from simple writing to formal ordination reveals its flexibility in conveying both literal and figurative senses of prior establishment.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding προγράφω enriches our grasp of Scripture as divinely inspired and purposefully arranged. The notion of writings "ordained" or "written before" underscores that God's revelation is not accidental but intentionally set forth for our instruction and salvation. This affirms the trustworthiness and sovereign planning behind the biblical text, encouraging believers to see the Scriptures as a foundation for hope and faith. The word also points to Christ as one who was "proclaimed" or "set forth" beforehand, emphasizing the fulfillment of God's redemptive plan revealed through the written word.
keyVerseReflection: Romans 15:4 states, "For whatsoever things were written aforetime were written for our learning, that we through patience and comfort of the scriptures might have hope." The use of προγράφω here stresses that the Scriptures were written in advance with deliberate purpose, serving as a foundation for teaching and encouragement. It highlights the intentionality behind God's Word as a source of perseverance and hope, reminding believers that the promises and lessons recorded previously remain relevant and trustworthy for present faith.
